content: Passivation refers to the process of rendering a material passive in its interaction with another material before they are used together. For instance, when preparing an aluminum container to store hydrogen peroxide, the container can be passivated by rinsing it with a dilute solution of nitric acid and peroxide, alternating with deionized water. The nitric acid and peroxide serve to oxidize and dissolve any impurities on the inner surface of the container, while the deionized water removes the acid and oxidized impurities. Another common passivation process involves cleaning stainless steel tanks. This is typically achieved by cleaning with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and citric acid, followed by treatment with nitric acid (up to 20% concentration at 120°F) and a thorough water rinse. In the context of corrosion, passivation is the spontaneous formation of a hard, non-reactive surface film that prevents further corrosion. This protective layer is usually composed of oxides or nitrides and is only a few atoms thick. Under normal conditions of pH and oxygen concentration, materials such as aluminum, iron, zinc, magnesium, copper, stainless steel, titanium, and silicon exhibit passivation. Ordinary steel can also form a passivating layer in alkaline environments, as seen with rebar in concrete. The conditions required for passivation are documented in Pourbaix diagrams. Additionally, certain corrosion inhibitors facilitate the formation of a passivation layer on metal surfaces. Some compounds, such as chromates and molybdates, dissolve in solutions and form non-reactive, low-solubility films on metal surfaces, contributing to electrochemical passivation. Specific materials can undergo tailored passivation processes. For example, aluminum can be protected from oxidation through anodizing, alodizing (also known as Alodining), or similar techniques. Stacked passivation methods are often employed for enhanced protection. Chromating, for instance, is frequently used as a sealant on anodized aluminum surfaces to improve resistance to saltwater exposure, nearly doubling the protection compared to anodizing alone. Iron-based materials, including steel, can be passivated by promoting oxidation (rust formation) and subsequently converting the oxidation to a metal phosphate using phosphoric acid. This can be further protected by surface coatings. Since the uncoated surface is water-soluble, a preferred method involves forming manganese or zinc compounds through a process known as Parkerizing. Older, less effective electrochemical conversion coatings include bluing, also referred to as black oxide. Nickel can be used to handle elemental fluorine due to the formation of a passivation layer of nickel fluoride. Bluing, also known as black oxide or browning (in historical contexts), is one of the oldest passivation processes for iron and steel surfaces. Newer proprietary processes for conversion coatings include Parkerizing for steel (dating back to around 1912) and Alodine for aluminum. Both are trademarked processes now owned by Henkel Surface Technologies. Chem film refers to any generic chromate conversion coating used to passivate aluminum. However, chromate coatings can also be applied to a broader range of metals and alloys. In recent years, chromate coatings have become less popular due to environmental concerns associated with their use. Iridite is another trademarked family of proprietary conversion coatings owned by MacDermid. Competing conversion coatings for aluminum, which address some environmental concerns, often appear as a slightly yellowish coating, similar in color to a yellow highlighter pen. Aluminum naturally forms an oxide layer almost immediately, which protects it from further oxidation in many environments. However, this naturally occurring oxide layer offers no protection in saltwater spray environments, such as those near bodies of saltwater. In such coastal environments, unprotected aluminum will corrode, turn white, and degrade significantly over a few years. To prevent this, a more robust conversion coating must be applied to aluminum surfaces to resist the saltwater atmosphere. Coatings such as Alodine, Iridite, and chem film provide varying levels of protection for aluminum surfaces. For further guidance on passivating stainless steel parts, ASTM A967 offers detailed recommendations.
